title: Agitation at the Community Clinic
objective: Students recognise lithium toxicity beneath a manic presentation, identify deficient fluid volume from vomiting as the priority nursing problem driving it, withhold the drug and escalate, monitor fluid balance, and evaluate the response.
endpoint: Stabilisation after overnight hospital treatment, clinic review, and client and family education

opening.narrative: Tanisha, a 34-year-old woman, is brought to the community mental health clinic by her sister after five days of sleeping very little, talking rapidly, and spending a large sum of money at the market. Her sister states, "She has not been herself. She argues with everyone and will not sit down." History includes bipolar disorder, treated with lithium carbonate taken at 10 am and 10 pm. Two weeks ago her dose was increased from 300 mg to 450 mg twice daily because she had begun sleeping less. She has no other prescribed medication and no known drug allergies. She lives with her sister and works at a grocery. The clinic's standing orders allow the registered nurse to withhold a prescribed dose and notify the physician when a drug level is markedly abnormal.

medications.name: Lithium carbonate
medications.status: Dose increased from 300 mg two weeks ago; last dose 10 pm yesterday; next due 10:00 am

stages.narrative: The nurse completes the initial assessment and sends blood for a serum lithium level at 9:40 am.

assessment.finding: Alert and oriented. Pupils equal and reactive to light. Coarse tremor of both hands. Walks with an unsteady, wide-based gait.
Heart sounds regular, no murmur. Peripheral pulses present. Capillary refill 2 seconds.
Chest clear with equal air entry bilaterally. No shortness of breath.
Abdomen soft, non-tender, bowel sounds present.
Passed a small amount of dark urine early this morning, the first since yesterday afternoon. No pain on passing urine.
Full range of movement in all limbs. No joint swelling or muscle tenderness.
Skin warm and intact. Lips and oral mucosa slightly dry.
Speech rapid and difficult to interrupt. Moves constantly in the chair.

stages.narrative: The sister adds that Tanisha has had two days of vomiting, has kept little down, and has been drinking very little fluid. She took her 10 pm lithium dose last night.
The serum lithium result is reported. The sample was taken about 12 hours after last night's dose. Tanisha's 10:00 am lithium dose is now due, and the physician is being contacted by telephone.

medications.name: Lithium carbonate
medications.status: Last dose 10 pm yesterday; 10:00 am dose due now

stages.narrative: The physician's working diagnosis is lithium toxicity, precipitated by dehydration from two days of vomiting. The physician confirms that lithium is to be withheld and arranges overnight admission to the district hospital for intravenous fluids, with urine output and electrolytes monitored. A clinic review is booked for the next morning, after discharge from hospital.

medications.name: Lithium carbonate
medications.status: 10:00 am dose held; withheld on the physician's order

medications.name: Sodium chloride 0.9%
medications.frequency: Over 4 hours, then rate as ordered by the admitting team
medications.status: Ordered; to start on admission to the district hospital

stages.narrative: Tanisha is discharged from the district hospital early in the morning and attends the clinic review with her sister. She received intravenous fluids overnight, and lithium was withheld.

assessment.finding: Alert and oriented. Hand tremor much reduced since yesterday. Gait steady.
Heart sounds regular, no murmur. Peripheral pulses present. Capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Chest clear with equal air entry bilaterally. No shortness of breath.
Abdomen soft, non-tender, bowel sounds present. No vomiting overnight; ate breakfast.
Urine output since yesterday approximately 50 mL/hr.
Full range of movement in all limbs. No joint swelling or muscle tenderness.
Skin warm and intact. Oral mucosa moist.
Slept six hours overnight. Still speaks rapidly but sits calmly during the interview.

medications.name: Lithium carbonate
medications.status: On hold since 10:00 am yesterday; no doses taken in hospital

stages.narrative: The sister quietly tells the nurse, "I love her, but I honestly cannot manage another week like the last one at home."
The physician restarts lithium at a lower dose, with a repeat level booked in five days. As she prepares to go home, Tanisha asks the nurse, "What can I do to stop this from happening again?"

medications.name: Lithium carbonate
medications.status: New dose ordered today; first dose 10 pm tonight; repeat lithium level in five days

questions.stem: Which finding should the nurse recognize as requiring immediate follow-up?

options.label: A
options.text: Pulse of 104/min while seated

options.label: B
options.text: Coarse hand tremor with unsteady gait

options.label: C
options.text: Blood pressure of 138/88 mm Hg

options.label: D
options.text: Irritability with reduced sleep

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Tanisha takes lithium, a drug with a narrow therapeutic range, and her dose was raised two weeks ago. A fine tremor is common at usual levels, but a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait is a neurological sign of a rising lithium level, so it needs follow-up now. The rest of the picture (restlessness, rapid speech, reduced sleep) is explained by the mania her sister describes.

distractor_rationales.A: A pulse of 104/min can be explained at this point by her agitation and constant movement. It should be rechecked as more history emerges, but on its own it does not point to a medication-safety problem the way the tremor and gait do.
distractor_rationales.C: A blood pressure of 138/88 mm Hg is only slightly raised and fits her agitation. Rechecking it later is reasonable; it is not the finding that needs action first.
distractor_rationales.D: Irritability and reduced sleep are the presenting manic picture already reported by her sister at 9:15 am, so they add nothing new requiring immediate follow-up.

questions.self_test: The pulse of 104/min is explained by agitation, whereas a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait in a client taking lithium signals a rising drug level.

meta.priority_principle: Medication safety cue over expected disease features
meta.prerequisites: Lithium therapeutic index; fine versus coarse tremor; signs of mania
meta.suggested_review: Lithium adverse effects and toxicity signs

questions.stem: How should the nurse interpret the significance of the vomiting and low fluid intake for Tanisha's tremor?

options.label: A
options.text: Fluid and sodium loss reduce lithium excretion, so the level rises

options.label: B
options.text: Vomiting has reduced lithium absorption, so the level is likely low

options.label: C
options.text: Dehydration alone is causing the tremor and needs replacing first

options.label: D
options.text: The tremor reflects anxiety about the vomiting, not the medication

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The kidneys reabsorb lithium by the same route as sodium. Two days of vomiting and little fluid have left Tanisha short of fluid and sodium, so her kidneys hold on to sodium and lithium with it. Together with the dose increase two weeks ago, this explains how her level could rise and produce the coarse tremor and unsteady gait.

distractor_rationales.B: Vomiting soon after a dose can lose some of it, which is why this is tempting. But two days of poor intake on a recently increased dose make accumulation the danger, and a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait points to a high level, not a low one.
distractor_rationales.C: Dehydration does need correcting, but it is the reason lithium is accumulating, not the cause of the tremor itself. Treating it as the whole explanation misses the drug level.
distractor_rationales.D: Anxiety can cause a fine tremor, but not a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait, and the vomiting and low intake give a clear drug-related explanation.

questions.self_test: Less lithium absorbed sounds logical, but the kidneys retaining more lithium during fluid and sodium loss is what makes the level rise.

meta.priority_principle: Link new cues to the drug's known risks
meta.prerequisites: Sodium and lithium reabsorption in the kidney

questions.stem: Before the lithium result is available, which nursing diagnosis should the nurse prioritize for Tanisha?

options.label: A
options.text: Risk for falls related to an unsteady, wide-based gait and constant restlessness in the clinic

options.label: B
options.text: Disturbed sleep pattern related to manic hyperactivity, as evidenced by five nights of little sleep

options.label: C
options.text: Risk for other-directed violence related to irritability and arguing with family members

options.label: D
options.text: Deficient fluid volume related to vomiting and poor intake, as evidenced by dry mucosa and scant urine

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Two days of vomiting with little fluid, dry lips and oral mucosa, scant dark urine since yesterday afternoon and a pulse of 104/min show an actual fluid deficit, a circulation problem that comes first. It is also the problem driving the danger: as Q2 showed, fluid and sodium loss make the kidneys hold on to lithium, so the coarse tremor and unsteady gait, and later confusion and seizures, will worsen unless the deficit is corrected. Treating it treats the presentation and its cause together.

distractor_rationales.A: Her unsteady, wide-based gait does put her at risk of falling, and she needs supervision when she walks. But fall precautions only guard against one consequence of the neurological signs; they do nothing to stop the level rising towards confusion and seizures. That rise is driven by the fluid deficit, an actual circulation problem, so it comes first, and in a supervised clinic the fall risk is readily managed alongside it.
distractor_rationales.B: Five nights of little sleep is real and will need attention, but it reflects the manic illness that is already known. It is not a threat to circulation or safety in the next few hours.
distractor_rationales.C: She is irritable and argues with her family, but she has made no threats and has not harmed anyone, so the cues for this risk are weak. It ranks below an actual fluid deficit with physical signs.

questions.self_test: Risk for falls is supported by her gait, but fall precautions do not stop the lithium level rising, while correcting the actual fluid deficit does.

meta.subtopic: Deficient fluid volume in a client taking lithium
meta.priority_principle: Actual circulation problem before risk problems; treat the cause driving the danger, not one of its consequences
meta.prerequisites: Signs of fluid deficit; renal handling of lithium; NANDA-I diagnosis structure
meta.suggested_review: Prioritizing nursing diagnoses (ABC, actual before risk)

questions.stem: While the physician is being contacted, which nursing intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care for Tanisha's deficient fluid volume?

options.label: A
options.text: Encourage her to drink two litres of water quickly to flush out the lithium

options.label: B
options.text: Weigh her once a day at the same time to track her fluid balance

options.label: C
options.text: Record intake and output and recheck pulse and blood pressure half-hourly

options.label: D
options.text: Keep her nil by mouth until the vomiting has completely stopped

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The level of 2.0 mmol/L, taken 12 hours after a dose, confirms that the fluid deficit has let lithium build up. For deficient fluid volume the nurse tracks the deficit closely: every drink, every episode of vomiting and every void, with pulse and blood pressure every half hour while she waits in the clinic. Urine output matters doubly because lithium leaves the body in the urine, and the record gives the physician the data needed to plan fluid replacement.

distractor_rationales.A: She has been vomiting for two days, so a large volume of plain water taken quickly is likely to come back up, and water alone does not replace the sodium her kidneys need to let go of lithium.
distractor_rationales.B: Daily weight is a sound measure of fluid balance over days, but it cannot show what is happening over the next hour or two while her level is 2.0 mmol/L, she may keep vomiting, and she is waiting to be transferred.
distractor_rationales.D: Withholding all fluids would deepen the deficit that is causing lithium to build up; the plan should measure and replace fluid, not stop it.

questions.self_test: Daily weight tracks fluid balance over days, but a client with a lithium level of 2.0 mmol/L needs her intake, output, pulse and blood pressure followed every half hour until transfer.

meta.subtopic: Monitoring deficient fluid volume in lithium toxicity
meta.priority_principle: Monitor the priority problem closely enough to detect change and escalate
meta.prerequisites: Intake and output measurement; signs of fluid deficit; lithium excretion
meta.suggested_review: Nursing interventions for deficient fluid volume

questions.stem: The physician has not yet been reached and the 10:00 am dose is due. Which action should the nurse perform first?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the 10:00 am dose while awaiting the physician's reply

options.label: B
options.text: Encourage oral fluids at home and reassess in the morning

options.label: C
options.text: Hold the 10:00 am dose and report the level and findings

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat the lithium level before deciding about the dose

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The clinic's standing orders allow the nurse to withhold a dose when a level is markedly abnormal. Holding the 10:00 am dose stops more lithium entering a toxic client, and reporting the level, tremor, gait and vomiting gives the physician what is needed to order treatment.

distractor_rationales.A: Giving lithium at a level of 2.0 mmol/L with neurological signs adds to the toxicity and risks seizures. Waiting for the physician is not a reason to give it.
distractor_rationales.B: Sending her home with oral fluids delays treatment of a toxic level and leaves the physician uninformed.
distractor_rationales.D: The level was taken correctly, 12 hours after a dose, and matches her signs. Repeating it delays the decision while the dose is due now; holding the dose and reporting comes first.

questions.self_test: Repeating the level feels careful, but the result already fits her signs and the dose is due now, so holding it and reporting comes first.

meta.subtopic: Holding a dose under standing orders
meta.suggested_review: When a nurse may withhold a prescribed dose

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that care for Tanisha's deficient fluid volume has been effective?

options.label: A
options.text: Sleeping six hours overnight in hospital

options.label: B
options.text: Sister reports that Tanisha's mood seems brighter

options.label: C
options.text: Blood pressure of 128/80 mm Hg

options.label: D
options.text: About 50 mL of urine an hour and a moist mouth

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The priority nursing problem was deficient fluid volume, so its outcome measures are urine output, mucous membranes and pulse. A urine output of about 50 mL/hr, moist oral mucosa and a pulse that has fallen from 104 to 88/min show the deficit is corrected. With volume restored the kidneys clear lithium again, which is why her level has fallen to 1.1 mmol/L and the tremor has eased.

distractor_rationales.A: Better sleep is a welcome sign that the mania is settling, but sleep does not measure whether her fluid deficit has been corrected.
distractor_rationales.B: A brighter mood is reported by her sister, but mood reflects the bipolar illness and changes over days to weeks; it says nothing about her fluid balance.
distractor_rationales.C: Her blood pressure was never low, and the small fall from 138/88 mm Hg fits her being calmer; it is not the measure of fluid replacement in her case.

questions.self_test: Six hours of sleep shows the mania settling, but only urine output, a moist mouth and a slower pulse show the fluid deficit is corrected.

meta.priority_principle: Evaluate the outcome the nursing diagnosis targeted
meta.prerequisites: Expected outcomes for deficient fluid volume; lithium level trends
meta.suggested_review: Evaluating fluid replacement and monitoring after lithium toxicity

questions.stem: Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: "That sounds exhausting. Tell me what a typical day has been like at home."

options.label: B
options.text: "She will settle once the medication takes effect, so give it a little more time."

options.label: C
options.text: "Would it help if we arranged for her to be admitted so you can rest?"

options.label: D
options.text: "Try to stay positive, because your attitude will influence her recovery."

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The sister is telling the nurse she is close to her limit. Acknowledging that feeling and asking what a typical day looks like keeps her talking and shows the nurse what support is needed (sleep, safety, money), which matters in the Caribbean where family is usually the main carer.

distractor_rationales.B: This offers reassurance with an uncertain timeline and passes over the strain she has just described.
distractor_rationales.C: Admission or respite may be needed, but offering a solution before understanding her situation is premature.
distractor_rationales.D: This puts the responsibility for Tanisha's recovery on her sister's attitude, which can add guilt to her exhaustion.

questions.self_test: Offering admission may be needed later, but it jumps to a solution before the nurse understands what the sister is struggling with.

meta.suggested_review: Carer strain in serious mental illness

questions.stem: Which instruction is most important for the nurse to provide?

options.label: A
options.text: Use ibuprofen rather than paracetamol for aches and pains

options.label: B
options.text: Keep your fluid and salt intake consistent every day

options.label: C
options.text: If you miss a dose, take two tablets at the next dose time

options.label: D
options.text: Choose low-sodium foods to protect your heart long-term

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: This episode happened because vomiting and poor intake lowered her fluid and sodium, so her kidneys kept more lithium. Keeping fluid and salt intake steady every day is the measure she controls that most directly prevents it happening again.

distractor_rationales.A: Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs reduce lithium excretion and can push the level up; paracetamol is the safer choice for minor pain.
distractor_rationales.C: Doubling up after a missed dose produces a peak in the lithium level and risks toxicity; the missed dose should be skipped or taken as advised.
distractor_rationales.D: Low-sodium advice sounds healthy, but cutting sodium increases lithium reabsorption, so it would make another episode more likely.

questions.self_test: Low-sodium eating is good general advice, but for a client on lithium it raises the drug level, so it is the wrong teaching here.

meta.priority_principle: Teach the cause the client controls

pathophysiology:
## Pathophysiology teaching

Lithium is cleared almost entirely by the kidneys. In the proximal tubule it is reabsorbed by the same pathways as sodium, so the body cannot tell the two apart.

Tanisha's dose had been increased two weeks earlier, which raised her level towards the top of the range. When she then vomited for two days and drank very little, she lost fluid and sodium. Her kidneys responded by reabsorbing more sodium to protect her circulating volume, and they reabsorbed more lithium with it. Her serum level rose to 2.0 mmol/L. The physician's working diagnosis was lithium toxicity precipitated by dehydration.

**Timing the level.** Lithium levels are read about 12 hours after the last dose. A sample taken a few hours after a dose reads falsely high, which is why the case states when the sample was taken.

**Signs.** A fine hand tremor is common at usual levels. As the level rises, it becomes a coarse tremor with an unsteady gait, then confusion, seizures and coma, and lithium can injure the kidney further, which slows clearance again. Mania and toxicity can occur together: the illness that prompted the dose increase has not yet settled, which is why her behaviour hides the drug problem.

**Priority nursing diagnosis.** Deficient fluid volume related to vomiting and poor intake, as evidenced by dry oral mucosa, scant dark urine and a pulse of 104/min. It is an actual circulation problem, and it is the cause the nurse can act on that keeps lithium in her body. Risk for falls, disturbed sleep and risk for violence are all supported, but they rank below it: fall precautions protect against one consequence of the neurological signs, while correcting the deficit (with withholding the drug) is what stops the level climbing towards confusion and seizures.

**Why each decision mattered.**
- Recognising the coarse tremor and unsteady gait (Q1) and linking the vomiting to lithium retention (Q2) pointed to the drug, not the illness.
- Choosing deficient fluid volume as the priority before the result (Q3) focused care on the problem driving the toxicity rather than the manic behaviour.
- Recording intake and output with pulse and blood pressure (Q4) tracked that deficit every half hour until transfer and gave the physician the data for fluid replacement; urine output also shows whether lithium is being cleared.
- Holding the dose and reporting (Q5) stopped more drug entering a body that could not clear it; the intravenous fluids then ordered restored volume and sodium so the kidneys could excrete lithium again.
- On day 2, urine output of about 50 mL/hr, moist mucosa and a slower pulse show the fluid deficit is corrected (Q6); the fall in lithium to 1.1 mmol/L and the eased tremor follow from it. Mood and sleep settle over days to weeks and measure the mania, not the fluid problem.

**Prevention.** Steady fluid and salt intake (Q8), avoiding NSAIDs and diuretics unless prescribed with monitoring, never doubling a missed dose, extra level checks after any dose change, and seeking help early when vomiting or diarrhoea stops a client keeping fluids down.
quality_report: Revised by Claude (2026-10-08) from Jade's Lithium Toxicity draft, at Ian's request, to meet V3 and the error-prevention addendum: Q4 changed from 'withhold the next dose' (duplicating Q5's key) to anticipating IV fluids with urine-output and electrolyte monitoring; a 10:30 am stage added so the IV fluids evaluated in Q6 are introduced first (V3 s.6); implausible distractors replaced (Q4 'increase the dose', Q5 'arrange transport before informing anyone', Q8 'stop lithium once stable'); Q1 rationale explains why the tremor is the safety cue. Cover, two-answer, cue-sufficiency and hidden-assumption checks were re-run on all eight items. Pending Jade's review and clinical validation (lithium thresholds, standing-order scope, Caribbean facility norms). Flow revision (Claude, 2026-10-09, at Ian's request): stages reordered so no question is answered by the screen before it (Q3 now asked before the lithium result; the standing-order wording moved to the opening; Q2 now analyses the vomiting cue). Clinical consistency: dose increased two weeks earlier explains mania with toxicity; coarse tremor and unsteady gait replace the fine tremor to match a level of 2.0 mmol/L; level timed 12 hours post-dose; overnight hospital admission made explicit; Q4 'withhold and repeat in a week' (half-right, overlapped Q5) replaced with activated charcoal; Q5 'half dose' replaced with 'repeat the level'; Q3 'worsening hypertension' replaced with an overactive thyroid. Revision (2026-10-12): added pain score to both vitals sets and SpO2 to day 2; expanded both examinations to all eight body systems in order (assess: normal cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, musculoskeletal findings, voided once this morning, lips and oral mucosa slightly dry to fit two days of vomiting; day 2: no vomiting overnight, oral mucosa moist); 'CNS' relabelled 'Neurological'. Medications charted: lithium carbonate 450 mg twice daily on the opening and as due at the level stage; 'held' status and the 0.9% sodium chloride order only at the transfer stage, after Q4 and Q5; day 2 shows lithium on hold and fluids completed; lithium 300 mg twice daily from 10 pm at discharge. No stems, options or keys changed. Jade to confirm: IV fluid regimen (1 L 0.9% sodium chloride over 4 hours then as ordered), the 300 mg twice-daily restart dose, and whether an antiemetic should be charted for the hospital stay (none added). Revision (nursing focus, 2026-10-12): Q3 rewritten as the priority nursing diagnosis (stem now asks for the nursing diagnosis to prioritize; four V3 s.13 options; key changed from B 'Lithium toxicity' to D 'Deficient fluid volume related to vomiting and poor intake, as evidenced by dry mucosa and pulse 104/min'; distractors Risk for falls (close), Disturbed sleep pattern (priority), Risk for other-directed violence (incorrect); new rationales, self_test and meta). Q4 changed from anticipating the medical treatment (key A, IV fluids with monitoring) to a nursing intervention for the priority problem: key C 'Record intake and output and recheck pulse and blood pressure half-hourly', different from Q5's key (hold the dose and report). Q5 unchanged (key C, hold the dose and report under the stated standing order). Q6 now measures the outcome for deficient fluid volume: key changed from A 'Falling lithium level with less tremor' to D 'About 50 mL of urine an hour and a moist mouth'; the lithium-level option was removed to avoid a second defensible answer; sleep (close), mood and blood pressure (incorrect) retained. Q1, Q2, Q7, Q8 unchanged. Narrative: the physician's working diagnosis (lithium toxicity precipitated by dehydration) added to the transfer stage, after Q5. Objective and teaching section updated to name the priority nursing diagnosis and link Q3-Q6 to it. Flow re-checked: Q3 is still asked before the level; no stage before Q3-Q6 states the diagnosis or the monitoring; Q2's key (fluid and sodium loss raise lithium) supports but does not state Q3's key. Jade to confirm: deficient fluid volume over risk for falls as the priority (the key assumes the fluid deficit, as the driver of toxicity, outranks fall risk in a supervised clinic setting), and half-hourly pulse and blood pressure as a realistic clinic frequency. Reviewer (2026-10-12): Re-tested Q3's key against a safety/injury diagnosis. Kept D (deficient fluid volume): it is an actual circulation problem and the modifiable driver of the rising level, whereas the only safety option, Risk for falls, guards against one consequence of the neurotoxicity and not the seizure risk; no Risk for injury option is offered, so A stays close but not defensible as best. Strengthened D's evidence: the baseline genitourinary finding ('voided once early this morning', which is normal at 9:30 am) now reads scant dark urine, the first since yesterday afternoon, and D's 'as evidenced by' cites dry mucosa and scant urine instead of pulse 104/min, because Q1's rationale attributes that pulse to agitation; Q1's A rationale now says the pulse is explained 'at this point' and should be rechecked as history emerges. Q3 A rationale and self_test now explain why fall precautions don't address the neurological danger. Q4 rationale, distractor B, self_test and the teaching section now say 'every half hour until transfer' (was 'hour by hour', inconsistent with the key); half-hourly pulse, blood pressure and intake/output is realistic for the 30-60 minutes she waits in the clinic. Options are in V3 s.13 form (actual with AEB, risk without); Q4 (C, record intake/output with half-hourly obs) and Q5 (C, hold the dose and report) differ; no stage before Q3-Q6 states a key. Q4 and Q6 stems now name 'deficient fluid volume' instead of 'the priority problem', so they stand on their own for a student who chose differently at Q3. No keys changed. Jade to confirm: deficient fluid volume over risk for falls/injury as the priority, and whether a 'Risk for injury related to rising lithium level' option should replace Risk for falls (it would compete with the key, so it was not added).
